title: Will the iPad Ever Be a Worthy Mac Replacement?
body:
iOS 9 brought us multitasking on iPad. Here's how far we've come since.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                            
        
        
        September 10, 2026
            
            
                        Credit: David MAREUIL/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images/Lifehacker
                            
    
        
        Welcome to a new series called Apple a Day, where sites in the CNET family are sharing pieces of Apple content from our archives—an article, review and/or video—daily from now through late September. In addition to Lifehacker, this series will include pieces from our sibling sites PCMag, Mashable, CNET and Popular Science.For the first five years of its life, the iPad could only run one app at a time. Then, iOS 9 changed everything. That update, released 10 years ago this month, introduced multitasking to the Apple tablet for the first time. "Split View" let you run two apps side-by-side at once; "Slide Over" gave you quick access to a third app in an iPhone-style window; and Picture in Picture made it possible to watch a video while working on something else. In an article published at the time, these changes prompted Lifehacker to proclaim that "iOS 9 actually makes the iPad usable for work."In total, you could have up to four different windows on screen through this concoction of features, a huge improvement over the previous limit of "one." Coupled with the new keyboard shortcuts, iOS 9 transformed the iPad, and brought it closer to the laptop replacement so many users wanted it to be. "Closer" being the key word there. 
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Multitasking on iPad is still a work in progressWhile iOS 9 made it possible to focus on more than one app at a time, it didn't address other iPad limitations that made it difficult for computer users to fully make the switch. In the 11 years since that update, Apple has chipped away at those issues slowly but surely, while upgrading the iPad's hardware exponentially. In iOS 11, Apple made it easier to launch an app into Split View from the Dock, and introduced cross-app drag and drop. With iPadOS 13, Apple introduced a desktop-class version of Safari, and rolled out the Files app, which even supported hard drives and SD cards. iPadOS 15 improved Split View and Slide Over accessibility, and made it possible to multitask with multiple windows from one app. By iPadOS 16, it seemed like Apple had had enough of people complaining that the iPad wasn't enough like a Mac. This update introduced Stage Manager, which let users display and resize multiple floating app windows on screen. You could even connect your compatible iPad to an external monitor to run Stage Manager on both displays, just as you might connect a MacBook to a monitor. iPadOS 17 improved the experience again, adding support for FaceTime calls from external webcams, while last year's iPadOS 26 provided another overhaul, introducing the closest thing to a macOS-like window system yet, right down to the traffic-light window buttons. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
We're at the point where, on the surface, the iPad can be considered Apple's answer to the touchscreen computer, especially when paired with a keyboard and trackpad. But in practical use, it's evident the iPad still isn't a Mac, even in cases where the iPad supports the apps and utilities you use on Mac. iPadOS doesn't feel designed for computer tasks; it feels like computer tasks were retrofitted to iPadOS. That doesn't mean things like multitasking and file support aren't welcome features, but the experience isn't as refined as it is on macOS. What's more, there is evidence Apple agrees the two devices are just too different, as rumors suggest the company might release a touchscreen MacBook as soon as next year. For me, iPadOS still feels at its best when I use one app at a time. All the above efforts to change its nature aside, that's probably because the iPad was originally designed that way. 
            
                        
                
            
                    
                                            
                
            
                Jake Peterson
                                    Senior Technology Editor
                                
                                            Covering tech news, how-to guides, explainers, and more.

title: Apple's 'Reference Image' Preserves Your Original Photos (Even After You Edit Them)
description:

            Credit: Apple
body:
Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Apple
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Figuring out what’s real online is only getting harder, and AI watermarks can only go so far to identify fakes. But today, Apple introduced a new standard to at least help identify real images taken directly on an iPhone: Apple Reference Image. It won’t solve the problem of finding the truth online, but it could be a helpful tool towards that goal.
The new feature will be available on iPhone 18 Pro models to start. It works by taking signed sensor data from the camera and using it to create a reference picture that can’t be edited, alongside a version that can be changed. The idea here is to give you a version of the picture that’s authenticated at the moment of capture, which you can compare against any modified versions later.
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Credit: Apple
                    
    
This provenance metadata can be preserved through certain supported sharing methods, which for now means select other Apple devices can check their verification status. That doesn’t mean that anyone can check the veracity of an image—especially if the version that gets posted and shared is an edited variant—but it provides a tool for the person or organization that took the picture originally to offer proof of verification.
This tool comes alongside the announcement that Apple will soon add support for the SynthID standard. This will potentially help users identify when an image has been created or modified with AI. Apple joins a long (though not exactly comprehensive) list of major tech companies to support the standard, including OpenAI, Nvidia, and obviously Google, the original creator of SynthID.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
We’re still in the midst of a scattershot image verification ecosystem. Apple’s Reference Image is a clever implementation that gives the end user a signed original to compare a picture against, which is a step up from C2PA metadata that merely embeds information about an image’s origin. It’s still unclear how widely these verification tools will be implemented and how easy it will be for users to trace where an image comes from and how, precisely, it was modified, but still, something is better than nothing.

        Nintendo announced the new The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time at its Nintendo Direct event this week. And already, Walmart has the game available for $59.99 (originally $69.99) for pre-order. Judging by how fast other pre-orders for the new remake have been going since the announcement, I wouldn't be surprised if this pre-order deal sells out too. And you're unlikely to see another discount on this major Nintendo game like the one Walmart is offering.
The Nintendo Switch 2 The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition console does not come with the game, so you will have to buy a physical or digital copy separately. Nintendo announced that the first printing of physical copies would include a "textured foil cover art" while supplies last, but it's unclear whether this sale is for that version. No pre-order product page lists whether it's a foil version, but as long as you're pre-ordering, you improve your chances of being in that pool.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The game will release on Nov. 5, and it's a faithful remake of the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time with improved graphics, cutscenes with dialogue, new mechanics (Link can jump now), and other new additions. It would be inaccurate to call it a one-to-one remake. I'm hoping Nintendo finally gives us the Light Temple that the original game on the N64 could not fit in the game.         Samsung’s flagship soundbars have reached the point where the yearly upgrades are more about refinement than reinvention, and that is pretty much the story with the Samsung HW-Q990H. Right now, this 2026 model is down to $1,049.99 on Woot, which is its lowest price yet, according to price trackers. The same system is listed on Amazon for $1,697.99 (down from $1,997.99), so not only is the discount substantial, but Prime members also get free shipping (everyone else pays a $6 delivery fee).
Samsung kept the same 11.1.4-channel setup from the older HW-Q990F, including the soundbar, wireless subwoofer, and two rear speakers, but leaned harder into software this time around—features like the SpaceFit Sound Pro automatically adjust the sound depending on your room layout, and unlike some auto-calibration features that barely change anything, this one reportedly shifts the audio balance in noticeable ways. Sometimes it improves dialogue clarity and bass response. Other times, you may prefer tweaking things yourself with the built-in seven-band EQ. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The system also handles basically every major audio format, supports wireless Dolby Atmos with compatible Samsung TVs, and includes 4K 120Hz HDMI passthrough for people gaming on a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X. That said, while the bass is strong for a compact subwoofer, it compresses when you push the volume near maximum, so it's not perfect for huge spaces or people who want nightclub-level output. More importantly, if you already own the HW-Q990F or even the older HW-Q990D, upgrading probably will not feel dramatic enough to justify the cost. But for someone starting from TV speakers or an entry-level soundbar, this system can completely change how movies, games, and even sports feel at home.

    Table of Contents
    
        
        At $154.99 for the Wi-Fi model, Apple’s refurbished 9th-generation iPad lands in the same price range as many budget Android tablets while still offering the polished experience people usually expect from an iPad. The Wi-Fi + Cellular version is probably the better value here since it costs only $15 more—and having built-in cellular connectivity means you are not constantly depending on public Wi-Fi or tethering from your phone, which makes a noticeable difference for commuters, students, rideshare drivers, and frequent travelers.And since Apple still supports this model with iPadOS 26 updates, you're not immediately stepping into outdated software either. That, combined with the “Grade A” refurbished condition (comes with little to no cosmetic wear) and included one-year warranty, still makes this older iPad a reasonable option for students, parents, travelers, or anyone looking for a dependable secondary device for reading, streaming, video calls, light work, and casual gaming. That said, it is not built for demanding creative workloads like professional video editing or heavy multitasking, but that limitation feels reasonable considering the price. The biggest compromise is the 64GB storage capacity, which works best for people who mostly stream content rather than store large games or video files locally.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
And while its A13 Bionic chip is older by Apple standards, it still keeps up with everyday use—apps launch quickly, Safari browsing stays smooth with multiple tabs open, and streaming services run without feeling sluggish. The 10.2-inch Retina display also holds up surprisingly well for everyday use, especially for reading articles and ebooks or watching videos. You still get Touch ID in the home button, stereo speakers, and support for the first-generation Apple Pencil for handwritten notes or sketching. Battery life also remains practical, with Apple estimating up to 10 hours of use on a charge, which is enough for a full day of browsing, streaming, and light work. All things considered, this 9th-gen iPad is a great deal.

title: iPhones Are Getting More Expensive, but AirPods Are Cheaper Than Ever
body:
Khamosh Pathak
                            
        
            Khamosh Pathak
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceKhamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 9, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Apple
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple is increasing the price of all existing iPhone models, including iPhone 17e, iPhone 16, and iPhone 17.
                                            The newly released AirPods 5 are actually cheaper than the outgoing model.
                                            The Apple Watch series has surprisingly missed the price bump.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        RAMageddon is real, and it’s finally come for the iPhone. Thanks to the ever-increasing costs of memory and storage, the prices of virtually all tech products are going up. A couple of months ago, Apple increased the pricing for the Mac and the iPad, by a couple of hundred dollars. Now, it’s the iPhone’s turn: Suddenly, all the iPhones are now $100 more expensive than they were yesterday, and the newly announced models are $100 more expensive than last year.
But it’s not all doom and gloom. The new AirPods are actually cheaper, and mercifully, some Apple products remain the same price.The $100 iPhone bump
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Khamosh Pathak
                    
    
At the September keynote event, Apple introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max. The 18 Pro starts at $1,199 for 256GB storage, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is now $1,399. Both of them are $100 more than the starting price of comparable iPhone 17 Pro/Max models.
The price bump doesn't stop with the new phones: Apple has flipped a switch and bumped prices on all existing iPhone models by $100. While Apple did not introduce an iPhone 18, the price of the iPhone 17 has quietly gone up; it now starts at $899 for the 256GB model instead of $799. The older iPhone 16 model is now $799, while the "budget" iPhone 17e now sells for $699. Even the iPhone Air has gone up to $1099.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Apple Watch pricing stays the sameSurprisingly, the RAM and storage costs haven’t hit the Apple Watch yet, or, at least, Apple is willing to absorb those increases for these smaller devices. The Series 12 Apple Watch with a new S11 processor and on-device Apple Intelligence features starts at the same $399 price as the Apple Watch 11. The new Apple Watch Ultra 4 also remains at the same $799 introductory price as the Ultra 3.AirPods are now cheaper (and better) than everOne popular product escaped the price bump: I was surprised to see a new standard AirPods model at the iPhone 18 Pro keynote, but the price drop was even more unexpected. The base AirPods 5 now come with built-in ANC (which used to cost extra), along with better transparency and improved sound features, and they are just $129, the cost of the outgoing AirPods 4 without ANC. Apple does have a more expensive model of AirPods 5 that comes with a wireless charging case, better battery life, and an on-stem voice control feature for $149, or $30 cheaper than the outgoing AirPods 4 with ANC model.

title: Apple Just Announced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 9, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Apple/YouTube
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple officially announced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max on Wednesday.
                                            The new iPhones look like the previous generation, the iPhone 17 Pro, but have smaller Dynamic Islands and come in new colors.
                                            The iPhone 18 Pro series also comes with variable apertures for the first time on iPhone, which will improve light control and bokeh.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        The iPhone Duo will inevitably steal tech headlines this week. After all, Apple finally made a foldable iPhone to compete with options from Samsung and Google. But while an iPhone with two displays is novel and exciting, it's also going to be expensive. I imagine there are many in the market for a new iPhone who aren't interested in spending as much as $2,000. There are also likely customers who don't want a foldable iPhone, and would prefer the standard smartphone design they're used to. That's where the iPhone 18 Pro comes in. iPhone 18 Pro: DesignIf you have an iPhone 17 Pro, you might confuse it for the iPhone 18 Pro. Indeed, Apple hasn't changed the overall design much this year, which is to be expected. The iPhone 17 Pro refreshed the Pro iPhone design with its large camera bump and plane of glass for MagSafe charging. The 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max aren't much different—though now the metal is color-matched to the back glass.That being said, there are some changes here you may notice upon closer examination. Perhaps first you'd notice the 18 Pro's Dynamic Island is smaller than it has been on previous Pro iPhones. With it, you're able to run three tasks at once, rather than two. That may prove useful depending on what you're doing, or it may end up cluttering the top of your iPhone. 18 Pro users will have to be the judge. You'd also notice some new color options not available on the iPhone 17 Pro, which I'll cover below.    
The displays will remain the same sizes as last year—6.3 inches on the iPhone 18 Pro, and 6.9 inches on the iPhone 18 Pro Max. But now, these displays use a more efficient LPTO+ technology. iPhone 18 Pro: ProcessorLike the iPhone Duo, the iPhone 18 Pros come with Apple's new A20 Pro chip built on 2nm technology. The company touts how the new chip is great for processing AI on-device, with a six-core CPU, seven-core GPU, new Neural Accelerators, and a second Neural Engine. Apple focused on the A20 Pro's thermal cooling with the new vapor chamber in the 18 Pro. Apple says this means there are significant sustained performance improvements over the iPhone 17 Pro.    Apple says this chip has the fastest CPU in a smartphone, with 50% better memory bandwidth. But, as with all performance claims, we'll have to wait until testers try out the A20 Pro for themselves. Still, Apple's newest chips always improve on the previous generation by some degree, so it's safe to say the 18 Pro (and the Duo at that) will be the fastest iPhones yet. Apple also says the iPhone 18 Pro has 36 hours of battery life while streaming video, while iPhone 18 Pro Max has 45 hours. The company says five minutes of charging gets you six hours of video playback.   iPhone 18 Pro: CamerasPerhaps the biggest change for the iPhone 18 Pro this year is its cameras. Apple's Pro iPhones are known for their shooters, but for the 18 Pros, Apple has taken things up a notch. For the first time, these iPhones have variable apertures. When using the 48MP main camera, your iPhone can physically open and close its aperture to control how much light hits the sensor—up to 50% more light than before. That offers two benefits: In dim environments, you can let in more light than you normally could. You can also use the aperture to control the depth of field, or the background blur. A large aperture (more light) means a blurrier background, while a smaller aperture (less light) means a cleaner background. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Apple also introduced Pro Controls, which has been sorely missing on the iPhone. You now can control white balance and shutter speed, and check the histogram. This mode works for both photography and videography. There's now a new "smart focus tracking" feature that uses AI to keep focus on a subject. Photographic Styles get some additional upgrades and controls, and Time-Lapse also supports 4K. With the 18 Pro, Apple is rolling out a "reference" feature to ensure that an original shot can be confirmed if an edit is later made with AI. Apple calls this a "digital negative." iPhone 18 Pro: ColorsAs previously mentioned, the iPhone 18 Pro's colors may be one of the most recognisably "new" features of this generation. Apple is rolling out color options in "Burgundy," "Glacier," and Silver, though the first two may be the more distinct of the bunch. Still, it's more variation than we have on the Duo.iPhone 18 Pro: PriceEverything is getting more expensive, thanks to RAMaggedon, and the iPhone 18 Pro is no exception. Apple is raising the starting price this year to $1,199 for the 256GB model, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 for the 256GB variant. iPhone 18 Pro: Release dateApple says the iPhone 18 Pro will be available to preorder on Saturday, Sept. 12 at 12 a.m. PT (3 a.m. ET). The devices then go on sale Friday, Sept. 18.

title: The iPhone X Literally Changed How We Use Our Devices
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 14, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: AFP contributor / AFP via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Welcome to a new series called Apple a Day, where sites in the CNET family are sharing pieces of Apple content from our archives—an article, review and/or video—daily from now through late September. In addition to Lifehacker, this series will include pieces from our sibling sites PCMag, Mashable, CNET, and Popular Science.By 2017, some of us had been using iPhones for 10 years—a whole decade building muscle memory, all of it based around the Home button. Press once to go home; press twice to open the app switcher; long-press to call up Siri; press in tandem with the power button to take a screenshot: These actions became so innate, you didn't think twice about using them—at least, not until the Home button disappeared. 
That was the year Apple released the iPhone X, introducing the device's most radical change since its first iteration. (Perhaps only to be surpassed this year by the iPhone Duo.) It's funny to think about it today, but back in 2017, the iPhone X's single pane of glass was disruptive, to say the least. Where was the Home button? Without it, how could you do anything? That confusion inspired Lifehacker to publish "The iPhone X Gestures You Should Master," a guide to navigating your newly designed iPhone. 
We had to learn to swipe up from the bottom of the display to go home; to swipe along the bottom to switch from app to app; to swipe down from the top right to access Control Center; to swipe down from the top left to access Notification Center. We even had to relearn reachability: Instead of lightly double-tapping the Home button to bring the screen down, you had to swipe down on the bottom of the display. 
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Reviewing these things now, it all seems so obvious, even second nature. Nearly another decade has passed since we published that story, and by now, most iOS users are accostumed to a Home button-free life. But looking through the comments on this nearly decade-old piece, it's clear the transition was anything but smooth. One user complained about how smartphone gestures were making everything more confusing. Another bemoaned how switching between their iPhone and iPad meant jumping between two different gesture systems. Fast forward to 2026, and it's near impossible to imagine going back. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Apple didn't immediately stop making iPhones with Home buttons—it also released the iPhone 8 and 8 Plus the same year as the iPhone X—but the writing was on the wall. Soon after, only the SE line shipped with the old design, and even iPads adopted an edge-to-edge display. With the launch of the iPhone 16e in 2025, Apple officially retired the once-essential Home button. Though you can still buy and use second-hand devices that have one (the 2022 iPhone SE can even run iOS 27), it's clear the company has moved on, and the gestures once so foreign they once prompted us to publish a guide to their use are now as innate as doing things the old way. Perhaps in another 10 years, wearables and hand gestures will have changed everything again, and we'll look back with nostalgia on an era when we had to touch our devices at all.
